stories.headline: Somaliland Opens Jerusalem Embassy After Israel Recognition
stories.summary:
Somaliland, the self-declared breakaway state in the Horn of Africa, opened an embassy in Jerusalem on Monday during an official visit by President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi to Israel. The move follows Israel's recognition of Somaliland as an independent nation last December, making it the first country to do so. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu praised the decision to site the mission in Jerusalem rather than Tel Aviv, where most foreign embassies are located, calling it a recognition of Israel's "ancient capital."

The embassy opening deepens a relationship that has been building since Israel's controversial recognition of Somaliland. Earlier this year, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar made an official visit to Somaliland's capital, Hargeisa. The two sides discussed cooperation on access to Somaliland's potential natural resources, including rare earth minerals and oil, as well as strategic access to Somaliland's coastline near vital shipping lanes.

The move has drawn sharp condemnation from multiple parties. Somalia, which considers Somaliland part of its sovereign territory, called any engagement with the "secessionist administration" a violation of its sovereignty. The Palestinian Authority described the embassy opening as "a flagrant violation of international law," and dozens of countries including China, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and the African Union had previously criticized Israel's recognition of Somaliland.

The development carries broader geopolitical significance at a moment of intense focus on Middle East diplomacy. Israel's cultivation of Somaliland as an ally gives it a strategic foothold near the Gulf of Aden, a critical global shipping corridor, while Somaliland gains international legitimacy from one of its few formal state-level relationships.

stories.headline: U.S. Sanctions Collapse Cuba Tourism by 58% in Five Months
stories.summary:
The number of foreign visitors to Cuba fell 58.4% in the first five months of 2026 compared to the same period last year, according to figures from Cuba's national statistics agency, Onei. Fewer than 360,000 people visited the island between January and May as the Trump administration's intensified sanctions campaign targeted the tourism sector, a primary source of hard currency for the Cuban government.

Major international operators have withdrawn from Cuba ahead of U.S. government deadlines. Air Canada suspended all flights to Cuba indefinitely, citing "ongoing political and economic uncertainty," while Spanish hotel chains Meliá and Iberostar halted operations at a significant number of hotels ahead of a June 5 deadline requiring companies to cease doing business with Cuban military conglomerate Gaesa. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has accused Gaesa of concentrating profits for a small elite while repressing dissent.

The economic pressure has rippled far beyond the tourism industry. An effective oil blockade has caused widespread fuel shortages, paralyzing rubbish collection and triggering frequent, lengthy power outages. State media reported that the survival rate for children with cancer has fallen from 85% to 65% since January, when President Trump threatened sanctions on any country or company supplying Cuba with oil. Rare public protests have broken out on the island, where dissent typically carries severe criminal penalties.

The Trump administration frames the sanctions as necessary pressure on an authoritarian government that represses its own people, with Rubio making direct appeals to ordinary Cubans. Critics argue the measures are inflicting disproportionate harm on the Cuban population, pointing to shortages of medicines, food and even communion wafers as evidence that the pressure falls hardest on civilians rather than the ruling elite.

stories.headline: India Temporarily Bans Telegram Ahead of Medical Entrance Retest
stories.summary:
India's government has temporarily blocked the Telegram messaging app until June 22, one day after a crucial medical entrance examination is scheduled to be retaken by approximately 2.28 million students. The National Testing Agency (NTA) said the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology acted in response to organized use of Telegram by cheating networks to defraud candidates, including operators who allegedly demanded hundreds of thousands of rupees from students and families in exchange for purported access to exam papers.

The NEET-UG exam — the primary gateway to medical college admission in India — was cancelled after its May 3 sitting following widespread allegations of paper leaks that triggered protests across the country. The Central Bureau of Investigation has made more than a dozen arrests in connection with the fraud. The ministry also directed Telegram to disable its message-editing feature until June 30, saying it had been used to fabricate evidence of paper leaks.

The ban drew immediate criticism from internet freedom advocates and users who called it a disproportionate "band-aid solution" to a systemic problem of examination fraud. The platform remained accessible to many users in India hours after the government's announcement, raising questions about enforcement. Telegram had not issued a public response as of the time of reporting.

The NEET controversy is part of a broader pattern of examination integrity failures in India: a similar scandal involving alleged paper leaks and grace-mark irregularities roiled the same exam in 2024 and led to demands for the federal education minister's resignation. The episode has renewed debate about the NTA's capacity to securely administer high-stakes national examinations affecting millions of students.

stories.headline: Update: Netanyahu and Trump on Collision Course as U.S.-Iran Deal Takes Shape
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have virtually signed a memorandum of understanding with Iran to end the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports, reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and launch 60 days of nuclear negotiations, according to a senior U.S. official. The agreement marks a significant diplomatic turning point after months of military conflict that closed one of the world's most critical oil and gas chokepoints.

The deal has placed the United States and Israel on a potential collision course, as the agreement falls short of Israeli war goals. Israel had sought a more comprehensive dismantling of Iran's nuclear program and a permanent end to Iran's support for Hezbollah, neither of which is addressed in the current framework. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has not publicly endorsed the agreement.

Inside Iran, the government is framing the deal as a victory, with senior officials arguing that the U.S. and Israel failed to achieve their core objectives — regime change, destruction of Iran's nuclear program through military force, or severing ties to Hezbollah. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf called it "a long step towards final victory." However, hard-line critics within Iran's own system have called the draft a document that would make Iran "an American colony" and accused negotiators of defying Supreme Leader directives.

Despite Trump's declaration of the Strait's "opening," ship-tracking data shows only seven vessels have transited the waterway since the deal was announced, with roughly 580 ships still waiting in the Gulf. Security concerns, uncleared mines, and uncertainty over enforcement have created a wait-and-see mentality among ship captains, owners, and insurers, meaning the economic relief promised by the deal has yet to materialize.

stories.headline: Russian Warship Fires Warning Shots at British Yacht in English Channel
stories.summary:
A Russian naval frigate, the Admiral Grigorovich, fired warning shots toward a UK-registered yacht in the English Channel on Tuesday morning after the two vessels came into close proximity in foggy conditions. The incident occurred approximately 20 nautical miles south of the Isle of Wight, in international waters between the Isle of Wight and Normandy. A couple in their 60s were aboard the yacht, which had drifted toward the warship after setting off from the UK without engine power.

The Russian Defense Ministry stated its crew acted in "strict accordance with international shipping regulations," saying the yacht was on a "dangerous approach" and that warning flares and radio contact had been attempted before shots were fired from rifles into the vessel's path. The British Ministry of Defense confirmed the incident and said it was investigating, while a spokesperson noted the shots "were not aimed at the vessel" but were intended to prevent a potential collision. No injuries or damage were reported.

The episode comes days after Royal Marine Commandos intercepted a Russian shadow-fleet tanker carrying sanctioned oil in the English Channel — the first such operation carried out by the British military. British officials said they do not believe Tuesday's incident is directly linked to that interception. The Admiral Grigorovich had been monitored by HMS Tyne and HMS Mersey over the preceding weekend and is understood to have been assigned by Moscow to escort shadow-fleet vessels through the Channel.

The incident raises fresh tensions between London and Moscow at a time when European security nerves are already heightened. NATO sources had previously told BBC Verify that the Russian frigate had been operating in the area for an extended period, repeatedly resupplied by a repair vessel, suggesting a sustained and deliberate Russian naval presence in the strategically sensitive waterway.

stories.headline: Venezuela Signs Deal with GE Vernova to Rebuild Crumbling Power Grid
stories.summary:
Venezuela's interim president Delcy Rodríguez has signed an agreement with General Electric Vernova, the U.S. energy company's local branch, to rebuild Venezuela's electricity grid — a system in severe disrepair after years of underinvestment under Nicolás Maduro. Rodríguez announced the deal at a televised ceremony at the presidential palace on Monday, calling it "a historic step" toward restoring what she described as an essential public service. Power cuts in Venezuela currently last 10 hours or longer and affect major cities including Caracas.

The deal is the latest indication that Rodríguez, who was sworn in after U.S. forces seized Maduro in January, is actively opening Venezuela's economy to American investment despite having been a fierce critic of the United States under the prior government. The agreement was brokered under Energy Minister Rolando Alcalá, an electrical engineer appointed three months ago — a departure from six years in which the ministry was led by military officials who failed to address the grid's collapse.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Congress recently that free and fair elections remain the long-term answer for Venezuela's stability and its ability to attract foreign investment, though he acknowledged conditions for such elections must first be created. Critics of the Rodríguez government note that despite economic openings, the legislative, executive, and judicial branches remain largely unchanged from the Maduro era, and the electoral council is still dominated by Maduro loyalists.

The power grid deal follows other signs of deepening U.S.-Venezuela cooperation, including a joint military strike last week that killed the leader of the Tren de Aragua criminal gang, carried out "in full co-operation with Venezuelan security forces" according to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Analysts say the GE Vernova agreement, if implemented, could address one of the most persistent obstacles to Venezuela's economic recovery.

stories.headline: Ohio Governor Mike DeWine Calls for State to Abolish the Death Penalty
stories.summary:
Ohio Governor Mike DeWine, a Republican, called on the state legislature Tuesday to abolish the death penalty, citing evidence that capital punishment no longer functions as a deterrent to violent crime. DeWine said data shows the death penalty is failing to achieve the purpose he had in mind when he helped write the law that established it, making his statement notable as a reversal by a longtime law-and-order Republican.

Ohio has not carried out an execution since 2018, and the state has faced ongoing legal and logistical challenges in obtaining lethal injection drugs. DeWine's call adds his voice to a growing bipartisan movement questioning capital punishment's effectiveness and fairness, even as the federal government under the Trump administration has moved to resume and expand federal executions.

Support for abolishing the death penalty has traditionally been stronger among Democrats and civil liberties advocates, who cite concerns about wrongful convictions, racial disparities in sentencing, and the irreversibility of execution. Proponents of capital punishment, more commonly found among Republicans and victims'-rights advocates, argue it serves justice for the most heinous crimes and provides closure to victims' families — a view the governor's announcement is likely to challenge within his own party.

Ohio would join a growing list of states that have abolished or placed moratoriums on capital punishment if the legislature acts on DeWine's request. The governor's move is considered significant given his long conservative record and is expected to prompt debate in the Republican-controlled Ohio statehouse.

stories.headline: Update: Strait of Hormuz Remains Largely Closed Despite U.S.-Iran Deal as Ships Wait in Gulf
stories.summary:
Despite President Trump's announcement Sunday that the Strait of Hormuz would reopen following a U.S.-Iran deal brokered by Pakistan, ship-tracking data from MarineTraffic shows only seven vessels have transited the waterway since the agreement was declared. More than 580 ships — including roughly 250 tankers and 330 cargo ships — remain waiting inside the Gulf, with approximately 75 percent of tankers stationary near major oil export terminals in Saudi Arabia, Iraq, and the UAE.

Experts cite three major obstacles to resumption of normal traffic: security risks from Iran's months-long pattern of firing on unauthorized vessels, mines laid during the conflict, and unresolved toll and authorization procedures. Trump later walked back his declaration of an "immediate" removal of the U.S. naval blockade, saying American warships would remain in position until the deal is formally signed. Satellite imagery from June 15 confirms four U.S. warships remain near the blockade line at the entrance to the Gulf of Oman.

Shipping analysts describe a pervasive "wait-and-see" mentality among captains, owners, and insurers. "It would take an extremely brave captain to transit through the Strait of Hormuz, given the current state," said Martin Kelly of crisis management firm EOS Risk Group. Some analysts expect risk-tolerant operators to move first, potentially building broader confidence if early transits succeed.

The Strait of Hormuz is the transit point for roughly one-fifth of global oil and gas supplies. Its continued effective closure — even after a announced diplomatic breakthrough — continues to exert upward pressure on global energy prices and raises questions about whether the deal's practical implementation will match its diplomatic framing.

stories.headline: Japan Raises Interest Rate to 31-Year High Amid Iran War Energy Inflation
stories.summary:
The Bank of Japan raised its benchmark policy rate to 1 percent on Tuesday, the highest level since 1995, citing a surge in global energy prices driven largely by the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran. The decision marks a continued departure from Japan's decades-long era of near-zero rates, which were adopted in the 1990s to combat deflation following a collapse in asset prices. Japan's wholesale prices climbed more than 6 percent year-on-year in May, the fastest pace in three years.

Bank of Japan policymakers said the risk of a sharp economic deterioration had been partially offset by government measures cushioning households from high fuel costs, but warned that medium- and long-term inflation expectations had continued to rise. Governor Kazuo Ueda, a central figure in the rate decision, missed the meeting while hospitalized for treatment of an infected liver cyst. The bank said it would continue to assess whether upside inflation risks outweigh downside economic risks in determining future rate moves.

Japan depends heavily on Middle East oil and gas imports, making it particularly exposed to the Hormuz closure and resulting energy price spikes. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, a traditional advocate of fiscal stimulus who has historically opposed rate hikes, has not publicly criticized the BOJ's tightening path since taking office. Economists note the rate increase signals that Japan considers its post-deflation inflationary upcycle durable enough to warrant normalization of monetary policy.

The move is the second rate hike since Takaichi took office and reflects a broader global trend of central banks tightening policy in response to Iran-war-driven inflation. Higher Japanese rates increase borrowing costs for the government — which carries one of the world's largest debt loads — as well as for businesses, presenting a difficult trade-off for policymakers.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Administration Classifies Anthropic's Fable AI Model as Defense Munition, Forcing Global Shutdown
stories.summary:
The Trump administration has classified Anthropic's newly released Fable generative AI model as a dangerous munition under U.S. export-control law, prohibiting foreign nationals from accessing it. Released on June 9, Fable was reclassified just three days later. Unable to distinguish between domestic and foreign users, Anthropic shut off access to the model entirely, affecting users worldwide.

The administration's action sets a significant regulatory precedent at a moment when U.S. AI policy is still taking shape. Critics argue the move undermines the administration's stated goal of ensuring American AI dominance, by signaling to foreign governments and companies that building on U.S. AI infrastructure carries unacceptable political risk. "Don't build your future on U.S. AI" is the message some analysts say trading partners may take away from the episode.

Supporters of stricter AI controls argue that advanced generative models pose genuine national security risks if accessed by adversarial states, and that export-control authority is an appropriate tool to prevent technology transfer. The administration has separately disclosed 3,611 active or planned AI use cases across the federal government — a 70 percent increase from the final year of the Biden administration — reflecting both the scale of AI integration and the stakes of getting regulatory frameworks right.

The Anthropic case highlights the fundamental tension in U.S. AI policy between promoting commercial competitiveness and restricting potentially dangerous technology. Analysts warn that overly aggressive export controls applied to commercial AI products could accelerate efforts by China and other nations to develop independent AI ecosystems, ultimately weakening American influence over global AI standards.

stories.headline: AI Deepfakes Proliferate Across 2026 Midterm Campaign Ads With Little Regulation
stories.summary:
Artificial intelligence-generated deepfakes have become a widespread feature of 2026 midterm campaign advertising, with attack ads routinely placing candidates in fabricated and compromising scenarios. What once appeared a distant technological concern has rapidly normalized in American electoral politics, blurring the boundary between authentic and manufactured political content at scale.

The practice remains largely unregulated at the federal level. Some campaigns voluntarily disclose AI-generated content in their advertising, but no law requires them to do so. Democrats have stated they would pursue mandatory disclosure requirements if they retake control of Congress, while the current Republican majority has not advanced federal legislation on the issue. State-level rules vary widely and are inconsistently enforced.

Experts warn that the proliferation of AI-fabricated campaign content is eroding the informal norms that have historically governed political advertising, and risks deepening public distrust in electoral information at a moment when confidence in democratic institutions is already under strain. The Reuters Institute recently reported that global trust in news has fallen to a record low, a trend that AI-generated political disinformation is likely to accelerate.

The 2026 midterms represent the first major electoral cycle in which AI deepfake ads have appeared at significant scale in competitive races across the country. Campaigns, platforms, and regulators are each grappling with how to respond, with no consensus framework yet in place to govern disclosure, takedown, or liability for fabricated political content.

stories.headline: Trump-Endorsed Candidates Face Key Tests in Georgia and Alabama Senate Primary Runoffs
stories.summary:
Voters in Georgia, Alabama, Oklahoma, and Washington, D.C. headed to the polls Tuesday in a series of primary runoffs and elections that will determine party nominees for high-stakes Senate and gubernatorial contests. The results offer a fresh measure of President Trump's endorsement power heading into the 2026 midterm cycle.

In Georgia, Trump made a last-minute endorsement of Rep. Mike Collins in the Republican primary runoff to challenge Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, one of the most closely watched Senate races in the country. Alabama also features a contested Republican Senate runoff. Both states are considered critical battlegrounds for control of the Senate in November.

The primaries are seen as an early indicator of whether Trump's endorsement remains a decisive force in Republican primaries, following a mixed track record in recent electoral cycles. Results from the evening's contests were expected to set the table for the general election campaigns in earnest.

Washington, D.C. voters were simultaneously choosing party nominees for mayor and congressional delegate, adding a separate local dynamic to a busy primary night across four jurisdictions.

stories.headline: Hungary's Parliament Amends Constitution to Bar Orbán from Returning as Prime Minister
stories.summary:
Hungary's parliament voted Tuesday to amend the country's constitution, capping a prime minister's tenure at eight years and effectively barring former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán from ever returning to the role. The measure passed 135 to 50, pushed through by the Tisza party's two-thirds supermajority under new Prime Minister Péter Magyar, who swept Orbán from power in April's election.

The amendment applies retroactively to all prime ministers since 1990, meaning Orbán — who governed Hungary uninterrupted for 16 years — is permanently disqualified from the office. Magyar himself would also be limited to serving until 2034 under the same provision. The law requires only the signature of President Tamás Sulyok to take effect.

Orbán and his depleted Fidesz party voted against the measure and condemned it as political persecution. Orbán's former political director, Balázs Orbán, accused Magyar of 'using political power to exclude a political opponent from democratic competition.' Orbán himself wrote on Facebook: 'If I'm needed, I'll be here.'

The constitutional change is part of a broader effort by the Magyar government to dismantle institutions built during the Fidesz era, including the dissolution of Orbán's Sovereignty Protection Office and steps to reclaim state assets transferred to politically connected public trust foundations. The European Commission recently agreed to unlock €16.4 billion in previously withheld EU funds, contingent on anti-corruption reforms now moving through parliament.

stories.headline: Russian Putin Critic Shot Dead in Poland Near Belarusian Consulate; Two Belarusian Nationals Detained
stories.summary:
Polish police are investigating the execution-style killing of Russian artist and Kremlin critic Robert Kuzovkov, known by the pseudonym Semyon Skrepetsky, who was shot five times in a car park in the city of Białą Podlaską on Monday. The location — roughly 40 kilometers from the Belarusian border and approximately 600 meters from the Belarusian consulate — has drawn immediate attention from investigators.

Kuzovkov, 44, was known for caricatures mocking Vladimir Putin, Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko, and Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov. Video posted on social media showed him attending a Russia Day protest outside the Russian embassy in Berlin just days before his death, where he carried a painting caricaturing Putin and Stalin.

Polish prosecutors said an unidentified gunman shot the victim twice, then approached the fallen man and fired three more shots before fleeing. Two Belarusian citizens aged 33 and 37 were detained near the consulate, though their precise roles had not been established as of Tuesday. An autopsy is scheduled for Wednesday.

The killing raises immediate concerns about a state-directed assassination on European Union soil, echoing previous cases of Kremlin critics killed abroad. Polish authorities have not publicly attributed responsibility, and the investigation is ongoing.

stories.headline: SpaceX Acquires AI Startup Cursor for $60 Billion Days After Record-Breaking IPO
stories.summary:
SpaceX has agreed to acquire artificial intelligence startup Cursor in an all-stock deal valued at approximately $60 billion, the company announced Tuesday. The deal comes just days after SpaceX completed what is being described as the largest initial public offering in history, raising $75 billion to fund the company's expansion ambitions.

The acquisition is intended to bolster Elon Musk's artificial intelligence ambitions, folding Cursor's AI capabilities into SpaceX's growing technology portfolio. Cursor is a prominent AI-assisted coding platform that has gained significant traction among software developers.

The timing — capitalizing on newly available public capital within days of the IPO — signals an aggressive expansion strategy. The $60 billion price tag for a single AI startup underscores the extraordinary valuations being attached to advanced AI tooling companies amid fierce competition between major technology players.

The deal adds to a consolidating AI landscape in which large technology and aerospace firms are racing to acquire foundational AI capabilities. SpaceX's move into AI software via a major acquisition represents a significant strategic pivot beyond its core launch and satellite businesses.

stories.headline: Update: Israeli Strike on Beirut Threatens U.S.-Iran Peace Deal as Signing Ceremony Approaches
stories.summary:
The U.S.-Iran peace deal, brokered by Pakistan and set for a signing ceremony Friday in Switzerland, faces a serious test after Israel struck Hezbollah targets in Beirut, drawing warnings from Tehran that the attack could derail the agreement. The deal, described by Vice President Vance as "about a page and a half" and "very general," would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the conflict that began with the U.S.-Israeli strike on Iran on February 28, but leaves Iran's nuclear program issues deferred for later negotiations.

Iran has seized two cargo ships in the Strait of Hormuz in the days since the deal was announced, and Iranian officials have stated that Tehran will continue to assert the right to control passage through the waterway. The framework's vagueness on core issues has prompted skepticism from analysts, who warn that the gap between the two sides on nuclear matters remains wide and that the Lebanon dimension adds further instability.

Energy markets, which saw sharp swings following the February outbreak of hostilities, rose on news of the agreement but remain volatile. Experts caution that the war's economic impact on global supply chains will persist for months regardless of whether the deal holds.

The Israeli strike is the most significant new development since the deal was announced, as it introduces a third-party variable that neither Washington nor Tehran fully controls. Trump has urged Israeli restraint, but has not publicly condemned the Beirut attack, leaving the deal's survival uncertain ahead of Friday's scheduled signing.

stories.headline: Wyoming Becomes First U.S. State to Issue Its Own Stablecoin Cryptocurrency
stories.summary:
Wyoming has launched the first state-issued stablecoin in the United States, pegged at $1 and backed by state reserves, marking a significant experiment in government-issued digital currency at the sub-federal level. The move positions Wyoming — already a recognized hub for crypto-friendly regulation — as a potential model for other states considering their own digital currency programs.

Proponents argue that a state-backed stablecoin could streamline government payments, reduce transaction costs, and attract further financial technology investment to the state. Critics and financial regulators have raised questions about systemic risk, the adequacy of reserve backing, and how state-issued digital currencies would interact with federal monetary authority and any eventual federal stablecoin framework.

The development comes as Congress continues to debate national stablecoin legislation, and Wyoming's experiment could either accelerate that process by demonstrating viability or complicate it by introducing a fragmented state-by-state approach. Federal Reserve officials and Treasury Department watchers have been monitoring state-level cryptocurrency initiatives closely as the U.S. works to define its regulatory posture on digital assets.

The Wyoming stablecoin is being closely watched by other states weighing similar moves, as well as by international observers tracking the United States' evolving approach to government-backed digital currency.

stories.headline: Global Trust in News Falls to Record Low, Reuters Institute Survey Finds
stories.summary:
Public trust in news media has reached its lowest point since the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism began tracking it in 2015, with global trust falling three percentage points to 37 percent, according to a major annual survey of nearly 100,000 people across 48 markets published Tuesday. In the United States, trust stands at 25 percent overall and drops to just 15 percent among right-leaning Americans. The UK recorded a five-point decline to 30 percent — 20 points lower than a decade ago.

The report found that more than half of respondents now access news primarily through social media and video platforms, though confidence in those formats is even lower than in traditional news, at 22 percent. Trust in AI chatbots for news information stands at 20 percent globally, though weekly use of AI for news has grown from 7 to 10 percent overall and to 16 percent among adults under 35.

Among individual outlets, CBS News and Fox News each saw trust fall by 10 percentage points from 2025, while CNN dropped six points — suggesting the erosion is not confined to any single part of the political spectrum. The institute attributed the decline to audience anxiety, disengagement, and dissatisfaction with how outlets cover persistent issues including immigration, inflation, and international conflict.

Despite the erosion of trust, the report noted that support for impartial journalism remains high and largely stable, and that audiences appear open to new formats — suggesting the problem may be with execution rather than the concept of news itself.
